L702@P18: ELLEN CRAFT
L703@P18: Born c.1826. Died 1897.
L704@P18: Ellen Craft’s story is not only a piece of history, but also an exciting adventure story and a romance.
L705@P18: She was born in Macon, Georgia. Because her mother
L706@P18: was enslaved, the law said that Ellen Craft was also
L707@P18: enslaved. As an enslaved woman, she was treated
L708@P18: like a piece of property. She was even given as a
L709@P18: wedding present to a white woman, just as if she
L710@P18: were a set of china or a pair of candlesticks. When
L711@P18: she grew up, she fell in love with a man who was also
L712@P18: enslaved, William Craft. White owners did not allow
L713@P18: enslaved persons to marry, but Ellen and William
L714@P18: Craft were married secretly in a special ceremony.
L715@P18: During the ceremony, the man and woman who wish
L716@P18: to marry jump over a broomstick in front of their
L717@P18: friends and relatives.
L718@P18: Once they were married, ElIen and William Craft
L719@P18: yearned to escape slavery. They wanted to have
L720@P18: children, but they did not want them to be enslaved.
L721@P18: They planned for several years, saving money William
L722@P18: Craft earned as a carpenter. Then, in 1848, they made
L723@P18: their daring escape. It was such a courageous escape
L724@P18: that it gave them a permanent place in history. An
L725@P18: account of their escape was published in Boston in
L726@P18: William Lloyd Garrison’s abolitionist newspaper, The
L727@P18: Liberator. Here is an exact copy of the account:
L728@P18: different masters in the State of Georgia. Ellen is so
L729@P18: near white that she can pass without suspicion for
L730@P18: a white woman. Her husband is much darker. He is
L731@P18: a mechanic, and by working nights and Sundays,
L732@P18: he laid up money enough to bring himself and his
L733@P18: wife out of slavery. Their plan was without precedent, and though novel, was the means of getting
L734@P18: them their freedom. Ellen dressed in man’s clothing, and passed as the master, while her husband
L735@P18: passed as the servant. In this way they traveled
L736@P18: from Georgia to Philadelphia. They are now out
L737@P18: of the reach of the bloodhounds of the South. On
L738@P18: their journey, they put up at the best hotels where
L739@P18: they stopped. Neither of them can read or write.
L740@P18: And Ellen, knowing that she would be called upon
L741@P18: to write her name at the hotels, etc., tied her right Photo Credit: Sterling, Black Foremothers
L742@P18: The Liberator
L743@P18: January 12, 1849, Boston, Massachusetts
L744@P18: Here is a wonderful case — read it!
L745@P18: SINGULAR ESCAPE
L746@P18: Pineville (Pennsylvania) — January 4, 1849
L747@P18: Dear Friend Garrison:
L748@P18: One of the most interesting cases of the escape
L749@P18: of fugitives from American slavery that ever have
L750@P18-19: come before the American people has just occurred under the following circumstances. William and Ellen Craft, husband and wife, lived with 18  BIOGRAPHIES OF TWENTY-ONE NOTABLE WOMEN
L751@P19: hand up as though it was lame, which proved of
L752@P19: some service to her, as she was called upon several
L753@P19: times at hotels to “register” her name. In Charlestown, S.C., they put up at the hotel which Gov.
L754@P19: M’Duffie and John C. Calhoun generally make their
L755@P19: home, yet these distinguished advocates of the
L756@P19: “peculiar institution” say that the slaves cannot take
L757@P19: care of themselves. They arrived in Philadelphia in
L758@P19: four days from the time they started. Their history,
L759@P19: especially that of their escape, is replete with interest. They will be at the meeting of the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society, in Boston, in the latter
L760@P19: part of the month, where I know the history of
L761@P19: their escape will be listened to with great interest.
L762@P19: They are very intelligent. They are young, Ellen, 22,
L763@P19: and Wm. 24 years of age. Ellen is truly a heroine.
L764@P19: Yours truly,
L765@P19: Wm. W. Brown.
L766@P19: Ellen Craft (continued)
L767@P19: After their escape, Ellen and William Craft
L768@P19: traveled with William Brown throughout New
L769@P19: England, telling their story. Although women did not
L770@P19: usually speak at public meetings, Ellen Craft spoke
L771@P19: because everyone wanted to hear her version of the
L772@P19: story. After all, she was the one who had disguised
L773@P19: herself as a white free man when in fact she was a
L774@P19: black enslaved woman. She had had to cut her hair
L775@P19: and wear pants—something no woman at that time
L776@P19: would ever think of doing! Everyone was amazed
L777@P19: that she was so brave and so smart.
L778@P19: When Ellen and William Craft stayed in Boston,
L779@P19: they lived on Beacon Hill at 66 Phillips Street with
L780@P19: Lewis and Harriet Hayden, who had also escaped
L781@P19: from slavery and were leaders of the abolitionist
L782@P19: movement. Ellen Craft worked as a seamstress, while
L783@P19: William Craft ran a furniture store. In Boston, they
L784@P19: were finally married in an official ceremony.
L785@P19: However, in 1850, the Fugitive Slave Law was
L786@P19: passed. This law meant that escaped slaves could
L787@P19: be captured and sent back to the South to slavery.
L788@P19: The Crafts were very famous by now, and two white
L789@P19: men came from the South to try to recapture them.
L790@P19: After some very frightening days, they fled to Canada,
L791@P19: where they took a boat to England. They lived in
L792@P19: England for 19 years. They had 5 children, and they
L793@P19: continued to be famous for their brave escape. In
L794@P19: fact, Ellen Craft participated in a “living history”
L795@P19: event at a museum in London. She posed as part
L796@P19: of an exhibit about the Underground Railroad and
L797@P19: answered people’s questions because she wanted
L798@P19: the world to know the terrible truth about slavery in
L799@P19: the United States.
L800@P19: In 1869, the Crafts returned to Boston, and then
L801@P19: moved to Georgia where they founded a school.
L802@P19: At the end of her life, Ellen Craft lived in South
L803@P19: Carolina with her daughter.
L804@P19: by Mary Smoyer
L805@P19: Information about Ellen Craft was found at the Schlesinger
L806@P19: Library, Radcliffe College, and in Sterling, Black Foremothers
L807@P19-20: N.Y.: The Feminist Press, 1988.THE BOSTON WOMEN’S HERITAGE TRAIL  19
L808@P20: Places to Visit
L809@P20: Walk the Beacon Hill part of The Boston Women’s Heritage Trail or The Black Heritage Trail and be
L810@P20: sure to stop to look at the Lewis and Harriet Hayden House, 66 Phillips Street, where Ellen and William Craft lived when they first arrived in Boston.
L811@P20: Contact The Museum of African-American History
L812@P20: www.afroammuseum.org
L813@P20:  617-742-1854
L814@P20: for a guided tour of The Black Heritage Trail and the African Meeting House.
L815@P20: Things To Think and Write About
L816@P20: Ellen and William Craft founded a school. How would you design a school? What would the building
L817@P20: look like? What courses would you offer? What do you think is the most important part of school?
L818@P20: What rules would you have? What would you name your school?
L819@P20: Classroom Projects
L820@P20: BOARD GAME: Using one of the books about Ellen Craft’s escape, make a board game of her escape route.
L821@P20: Remember she traveled on a train.
L822@P20: There are three very good books about Ellen Craft’s escape.

L44: January 12, 1849
L45: 
L46: William Wells Brown writes to Garrison, telling of the escape of the Crafts, Ellen, 22, William, 24 years of age.  “They are now hid away, within 22 miles of Philadelphia, where they will remain until the 6th, when they will leave with me for New England.” Then Brown lists four days when he will lecture about the escape, in Norwich, Ct., in Worcester, Pawtucket, and New Bedford.
